title: Pressure in gases — molecules in motion
examTip: Gas pressure questions almost always want an explanation using the molecules. Say 'more frequent collisions with the container walls', not just 'molecules move faster'. And always check that a pV = constant question is at constant temperature.
introTips: Pressure is caused by gas molecules hitting the walls of their container. More hits, or harder hits, means higher pressure.
Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules. Hotter means faster.
pV = constant only works for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.
p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ is the equation you need. Know it and be able to use it.
intro: You see gas pressure at work when you pump up a bike tyre. You see it when you squeeze a balloon. You see it when a weather balloon grows as it rises. Gas pressure is not a mysterious force. It is simply huge numbers of tiny molecules crashing into a container's walls, again and again. Understanding this is powerful. You can predict what happens to the pressure when you heat a gas. You can also predict what happens when you compress it into a smaller space. Engineers use these ideas to design car engines, aerosol cans and scuba diving equipment.

keyPoints.heading: What causes gas pressure
keyPoints.content: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. Gas pressure is caused by gas molecules colliding with the walls of their container. Each collision pushes on the wall with a tiny force. Huge numbers of molecules collide every second. So the total effect is a steady pressure that you can measure. The pressure gives a net force at right angles to the wall of the container. This is true for any surface. Pressure = force ÷ area. So more collisions per second, or harder collisions, means higher pressure. Key idea: at a fixed volume, faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often → higher pressure. If you heat the gas, molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often → pressure rises (if the volume is fixed). Now compress the gas into a smaller volume. The same number of molecules are in a smaller space. They hit the walls more often per second → pressure rises (if the temperature is fixed).
writeBullets: Gas molecules are in constant random motion
Gas pressure — caused by gas molecules colliding with the container walls
Each collision pushes with a force. Huge numbers of collisions every second make a pressure you can measure
The pressure gives a net force at right angles to the wall (or any surface)
Fixed volume, higher temperature → faster molecules → harder, more frequent collisions with the walls → higher pressure
Smaller volume → same molecules in less space → more frequent collisions with the walls → higher pressure
Pressure = force ÷ area (Pa = N/m²)

keyTerms.def: The force per unit area exerted by gas molecules colliding with container walls
A molecule striking the container wall — each collision exerts a tiny force contributing to total pressure

keyPoints.memTip: More collisions OR harder collisions = higher pressure. Temperature controls speed. Volume controls how often they hit.
keyPoints.tutor_note: You need to link the cause (molecules colliding with the walls) to the effect (pressure) clearly. Mark schemes reward the phrase 'collisions with the walls'.

keyPoints.heading: Temperature and pressure at constant volume
keyPoints.content: The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. The hotter the gas, the faster its molecules move on average. Now keep the volume fixed, as in a sealed rigid container. Heat the gas, and its temperature rises. The molecules move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often. So the pressure rises. Cool the gas, and the opposite happens. The molecules slow down. They hit the walls less hard and less often. So the pressure falls. So changing the temperature of a gas at constant volume changes its pressure. You need to explain this in words, using the molecules.
writeBullets: The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules
Fixed volume, higher temperature → faster molecules → harder, more frequent collisions → higher pressure
Fixed volume, lower temperature → slower molecules → softer, less frequent collisions → lower pressure
Explain it in words: molecules, then collisions, then pressure

keyTerms.def: Related to the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules
The gas stays in the same space, for example a sealed rigid container

keyPoints.memTip: Hotter gas → faster molecules → harder, more frequent hits → higher pressure.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Say what happens to the molecules, then to the collisions, then to the pressure. Each link in the chain matters.

keyPoints.heading: Pressure and volume at constant temperature
keyPoints.content: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. Take a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature. Its pressure and volume are inversely proportional. So p × V = constant, or p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. If you halve the volume, the pressure doubles. If you double the volume, the pressure halves. Particle explanation: compress the gas into half the volume. The same number of molecules now have less space. They hit each part of the walls twice as often per second → pressure doubles. Let the gas expand into a bigger volume, and they hit each part of the walls less often. So the pressure falls. Units: pressure in pascals (Pa). Volume in metres cubed (m³). You can use kPa or cm³ if both sides use the same unit. Worked example: a gas has pressure 200 kPa and volume 3 m³. It is compressed to 1.5 m³ at constant temperature. Find the new pressure: p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂ = (200 × 3) ÷ 1.5 = 600 ÷ 1.5 = 400 kPa.
writeBullets: pV = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature. So p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
Pressure and volume are inversely proportional. When one doubles, the other halves
Halve the volume → molecules hit each part of the walls twice as often → pressure doubles
Bigger volume → less frequent collisions with the walls → lower pressure
Units: pressure in Pa, volume in m³. kPa or cm³ also work if both sides use the same unit
Rearrange: p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂ or V₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ p₂

keyTerms.def: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure × volume stays the same; p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
When one quantity doubles, the other halves — their product stays constant

keyPoints.memTip: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. Both sides equal the same constant.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Check that the temperature is stated as constant before you use pV = constant.

keyPoints.heading: Doing work on a gas
keyPoints.content: Work is the transfer of energy by a force. Push a piston into a gas, and you apply a force to the gas. You are doing work on the gas. This transfers energy to the gas. It increases the internal energy of the gas. This can make the temperature of the gas rise. Example: a bicycle pump. You push the handle in, again and again. Each push does work on the air inside the pump. The internal energy of the air goes up. Its molecules move faster on average, so its temperature rises. That is why the pump gets warm.
writeBullets: Work is the transfer of energy by a force
Doing work on a gas increases its internal energy
This can cause the temperature of the gas to rise
Bicycle pump: pushing the handle does work on the air → internal energy rises → temperature rises

keyTerms.def: The transfer of energy by a force
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles (atoms and molecules) in a system

keyPoints.memTip: Push on a gas → give it energy → warm it up.
keyPoints.tutor_note: For a pump question, follow the chain: force on the gas, work done, internal energy up, temperature up.

0.question: What causes the pressure a gas exerts on its container?
options: Gas molecules colliding with the walls
Gas molecules sticking to the walls
Gas molecules standing still and pressing on the walls
0.correctFeedback: Correct. The molecules are in constant random motion. Each collision pushes on the wall, at right angles to it.
0.wrongFeedback: Gas molecules are always moving at random. They collide with the walls, and each collision pushes on the wall. Together these make the pressure.

1.question: A gas is heated in a sealed, rigid container. Why does its pressure rise?
options: The molecules move faster, so they hit the walls harder and more often
The molecules get bigger and push on the walls
The molecules slow down and stick to the walls
1.correctFeedback: Correct. Faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often. So the force on the walls goes up, and so does the pressure.
1.wrongFeedback: Heating does not change the number or size of the molecules. It makes them move faster. They hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises.

2.question: A sealed container of gas has a pressure of 150 kPa at a volume of 4 m³. The gas is compressed to 2 m³ at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?
2.correctFeedback: Correct! p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ → p₂ = (150 × 4) ÷ 2 = 300 kPa. Halving the volume doubles the pressure.
2.wrongFeedback: Use pV = constant: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. Rearrange: p₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂ = (150 × 4) ÷ 2 = 300 kPa. When volume halves, pressure doubles.

3.question: You pump up a tyre quickly. Why does the air in the pump get warmer?
options: Pushing the handle does work on the air. Its internal energy rises, so its temperature rises
The air molecules get bigger as they are compressed
More air molecules are made inside the pump
The pump takes in heat from the tyre
3.correctFeedback: Correct. Work is the transfer of energy by a force. Doing work on the air raises its internal energy and its temperature.
3.wrongFeedback: Pushing the handle is a force on the air. That does work on the air, which transfers energy to it. Its internal energy rises, so its temperature rises.

commonMistakes: Using pV = constant when the temperature also changes. It only works at constant temperature.
Giving a vague reason for a pressure rise, like 'molecules move faster'. You must say 'more frequent or harder collisions with the walls' for full marks.
Mixing units in an equation. Pressure must be in the same units on each side: both Pa or both kPa. The same goes for volume.
Saying pressure goes up when volume goes up. It is the opposite. Bigger volume → molecules hit the walls less often → pressure falls.
examTips: Particle explanations must mention collisions with the container walls, not just how fast the molecules move. You need both parts for full marks.
For pV = constant answers, check: does the pressure go up when the volume goes down? If yes, your answer makes sense.
Write out the equation before you substitute. This gets method marks, even if you make a maths slip.
revisionCardBullets: Gas molecules are in constant random motion
Gas pressure is caused by molecules colliding with the container walls
The pressure gives a net force at right angles to the wall
Fixed volume, higher temperature → faster molecules → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure
Smaller volume → more frequent collisions per unit area → higher pressure
Fixed volume: higher temperature → higher pressure. Explain it with the molecules
Volume halves → pressure doubles (at constant temperature)
Pressure units: Pa (pascals). Volume units: m³ or cm³. Keep them the same on both sides
Doing work on a gas raises its internal energy. This can raise its temperature, as in a bicycle pump
